title: SRE: SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, and Runbooks (Standards & Playbooks)
author: Ari Chen
summary: This document defines Redwood Inference SRE standards for service-level objectives (SLOs) and error budgets, capacity planning processes, reliability initiatives, incident review expectations, operational tooling requirements, and runbook structure. It is intended for SREs, on-call engineers, service owners, and platform teams responsible for production reliability.
goals_and_scope: Goals: provide a consistent approach to defining SLOs and error budgets, standardize capacity planning, drive measurable reliability improvements through initiatives, and ensure incident reviews and runbooks are actionable and reproducible. Scope: all customer-facing Redwood services (hosted API, dedicated control plane, telemetry systems) and core platform components (routing, caching, serving runtime). Exclusions: one-off experiments or private PoCs unless they affect production traffic.
slos_and_error_budgets:
Overview:
- SLOs define user-facing reliability targets (availability, latency, correctness for model outputs where applicable).
- Error budgets quantify allowable shortfall and enable risk-based decisions (deployments, rollouts, model changes).
SLO taxonomy and examples:
- Availability (HTTP): 99.95% p99 success-rate per rolling 30-day window for hosted inference API routes serving production traffic.
- Latency: p95 tail latency <= 200ms for short-text generation routes (<=512 tokens), p95 <= 600ms for long-form routes (>512 tokens).
- Throughput/Capacity SLO: sustained request throughput at 95% of provisioned capacity for Dedicated pools (30-day rolling average).
- Model quality SLO (where applicable): automated eval set pass-rate >= 95% for critical prompt suites per release.
Error budget policy:
1. Measurement: error budget burn is calculated daily using the SLO window (30-day rolling unless otherwise specified).
2. Burn thresholds and actions:
   - Green (<=50% burn): normal operations; regular rollouts allowed.
   - Yellow (50-80% burn): require staging/limited rollouts for non-critical changes; optional manual review for high-risk changes.
   - Red (>80% burn): freeze risky changes (full-model rollouts, config changes that affect routing or capacity). Must convene reliability owners and open a mitigation plan within 1 business day.
3. Ownership: each SLO must list an SLO owner (product/service owner) and an SRE lead responsible for monitoring and mitigation.
4. Exceptions: temporary SLO adjustments require documented approval from product and SRE leads and a retro post-resolution.
SLO definition checklist (required fields for every SLO):
- Service name, route(s) or metric name, SLI definition, measurement window, target value, owner, alerting thresholds, burn-policy mapping, associated runbooks and dashboards.
Example SLO (plain text table):
| Field | Value |
| Service | hosted-inference-api |
| SLI | 5xx + client-visible errors / total requests |
| Window | 30-day rolling |
| Target | 99.95% success-rate |
| Owner | hosted-api-product-team |
| SRE Lead | Ari Chen |
| Alerts | page at 5% daily burn, slack alert at 2% burn |
capacity_planning:
Principles:
- Plan for peak plus safety: target N+20% buffer on GPU-backed serving capacity for expected traffic peaks for first 30 days after major launches.
- Distinguish elastic (autoscaling) vs. reserved capacity (Dedicated). Reserved capacity commitments must map to business contracts.
Capacity planning cadence and responsibilities:
1. Quarterly review: service owners + SRE review traffic growth forecasts, model size/latency changes, and commit capacity adjustments.
2. Pre-launch runbook: 30/14/7/1 day checks before major release (see checklist below).
3. Monthly utilization report: SRE generates per-pool utilization, tail-latency, and cache-hit-rate metrics.
Key thresholds and alerts:
- Provisioning alert: sustained pool CPU/GPU utilization > 85% for 30 minutes -> page SRE on-call.
- Latency buffer alert: p95 latency exceeds SLO by >20% for 10 minutes -> create incident and investigate throttling, batch size, or kernel hot-path regressions.
- Cache efficacy: cache hit-rate < 40% for critical KV caches -> schedule cache tuning and traffic analysis.
Pre-launch checklist (30/14/7/1 days):
- 30d: traffic forecast validated; capacity plan and budget approved; load test scenarios defined.
- 14d: preliminary load tests on staging; SLO smoke tests; monitoring dashboards created.
- 7d: runbook reviewed; on-call rotation confirmed; rollback and mitigation rehearsed.
- 1d: final smoke test; alerting verified end-to-end; deployment window confirmed.
Load-testing guidelines:
- Use representative traffic mixes including cold-cache scenarios and varying sequence lengths.
- Include KV cache warm-up, batch size tuning, and model-variant fallbacks in test scripts.
reliability_initiatives:
Strategy and example initiatives:
- Goal: reduce customer-visible incidents by 40% year-over-year and decrease mean time to restore (MTTR) by 30% within two quarters.
Priority initiative examples:
1. Adaptive autoscaling pilot: implement workload-aware batching + autoscaler to smooth GPU utilization and reduce cold-starts. Success metric: reduced 95th latency by 15% during bursts.
2. Prefix/KV Cache improvements: increase cache hit-rate for common prefixes; success metric: 25% reduction in token compute cost for cached flows.
3. Model rollout safety net: automated canary evaluation with quality SLO checks and automated rollback on regressions. Success metric: <1% rollout-related incidents.
4. Observability improvements: standardize high-cardinality tracing for inference requests with consistent trace ids and sampling. Success metric: incident triage time reduced by 20%.
Initiative lifecycle and measurement:
- Proposal -> experiment -> pilot -> org-wide rollout or retire.
- Each initiative must include: owner, hypothesis, success metrics, experiment timeframe, and post-mortem template.
incident_review_standards:
Purpose: ensure incidents produce clear, actionable remediation and prevent recurrence.
Severity classification (examples):
- Sev1: customer-impacting outage affecting >5% of production requests or complete regional outage.
- Sev2: significant degradation for a subset of customers or routes.
- Sev3: minor errors or increases in latency with limited user impact.
Incident lifecycle and required deliverables:
1. Triage & Severity declaration (within 30 minutes).
2. Post-incident report: must be published within 72 hours for Sev1, 7 days for Sev2/3. Report sections: summary, timeline, detection method, root cause analysis (RCA), mitigations taken, long-term actions (LTA), owners, follow-up dates, and retro notes.
3. RCA expectations: use the 5-whys and include evidence (metrics, traces, logs). Avoid blame; focus on systemic fixes.
4. Action tracking: create JIRA tasks for each LTA with SLA for closure (Sev1 LTA within 30 days).
5. Incident review meeting: include SRE lead, service owner, on-call responder, and product representative.
Postmortem template (plain headings to be used in the report):
- Title
- Incident summary (one-paragraph)
- Impact (customers affected, services affected, duration)
- Detection and response timeline (timestamped)
- Root cause
- Immediate mitigations
- Long-term actions and owners
- Metrics and graphs (links to dashboards)
- Lessons learned
operational_tooling:
Required dashboards and alerts:
- SLO dashboards: per-service SLI breakdown (availability, latency buckets, error budget burn) with 30-day and 7-day windows.
- Capacity dashboards: per-pool utilization, instance-level GPU metrics, queue lengths, and batch-size distributions.
- Incident triage view: correlated traces, top error types, and recent deploys.
- Runbook landing page: quick links to critical playbooks and contact lists.
Alerting standards:
- Alert fatigue management: threshold alerts for pages only when automated mitigation is unavailable or human action required. Use Slack/ops channels for lower-severity notifications.
- Alert ownership: every actionable alert must list a primary pager (team) and a runbook link.
Tooling stack (recommended):
- Metrics: Prometheus + Cortex for long-term retention.
- Tracing: Jaeger or Tempo with 100% sampling for on-call sessions and adaptive sampling otherwise.
- Logging: ELK/Cloud logging with structured logs and request id propagation.
- Incident/Pages: PagerDuty integrated with Slack runbook shortcuts.
- Load testing: k6 and a JMeter wrapper for complex scenarios.
Operational hygiene and automation:
- Automated runbook steps: where possible, instrument runbooks with one-click remediation for common actions (scale pool, restart service, toggle feature flag).
- Continuous improvement: weekly reliability digest summarizing alert counts, top errors, and suggested tuning.
runbooks:
Runbook structure (required for every production-facing service):
- Runbook title and service identifier
- Purpose and scope
- Pre-conditions and prerequisites
- Observable symptoms (what triggers use of this runbook)
- Immediate mitigation steps (numbered, with exact CLI/console commands and required permissions)
- Diagnostic commands and expected outputs
- Rollback and recovery procedures
- Post-incident cleanup and verification
- Contacts and escalation path
- Change history (who last edited and why)
Example immediate mitigation snippet (plain text):
1) Symptom: p95 latency > SLO and queue length rising on pool gpu-pool-24.
2) Mitigation:
   a) Run: `kubectl scale deployment gpu-pool-24 --replicas=6 --namespace=serving`
   b) Validate: `kubectl get pods -l app=gpu-pool-24 -o wide` and check `prometheus` panel for dropping queue length.
   c) If scaling fails, route traffic to fallback model variant: update routing via `redwoodctl route set --service=hosted-inference --variant=fallback-small`
Runbook review cadence:
- Minimum quarterly review by SRE and service owner.
- Any deployment that changes runtime behavior (batching, caching, kernel changes) triggers runbook re-validation before rollout.
ownership_and_communication:
On-call model and escalation:
- Primary on-call: SRE rotation (2-week shifts). Secondary/backup: cross-team SRE.
- Escalation matrix: on-call -> SRE lead -> eng manager -> platform director.
- Communication templates: incident start, incident update (every 30 minutes), incident resolved, and postmortem published.
Stakeholder notifications:
- For Sev1: notify execs, customer success for customer-impacting issues, and legal if data exposure suspected.
- For Sev2: notify product and account teams for impacted customers.
